summary: Explains the need for SIP URI-list services and sets out requirements for invoking them. It also defines a framework for these services, which includes security considerations that apply to them. URI-list services let a client send one request that a server distributes to many recipients. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Instead of mailing the same letter to fifty people yourself, you give one copy and a list of names to a helper who sends them all. This describes how that helper should work safely.

questions: send one sip request to many recipients
what is a sip uri-list service
what is the recipient-list content disposition
how do uri-list services prevent amplification attacks
subtitle: Requirements, a framework and security rules for SIP servers that fan one request out to a list of recipients.

tldr.problem: Sending the same SIP request to many recipients from a low-bandwidth link means repeating a large request many times from the client.
tldr.mechanism: A URI-list service in the network receives one request carrying or referencing a list of URIs and sends similar requests to each destination. A new recipient-list body disposition type carries the list.
tldr.outcome: Because one request becomes many, the service can be abused for amplification attacks, so the RFC requires authenticating the invoker and sending only to recipients who have opted in.

today: RFC 5363 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The per-method specifications it points to are RFC 5365, RFC 5366 and RFC 5367.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
Some applications need a SIP user agent to perform a similar transaction with many remote user agents. An instant messaging client that wants to send one message to n receivers would otherwise send n MESSAGE requests. If the request is large, the number of recipients is high, or both, the access network of the client carries a lot of traffic.

The answer is a URI-list service in the network. It receives a request that contains or references a list of one or more URIs and sends a number of similar requests to the destinations. It typically then informs the client of their status. In effect it acts as a B2BUA (back-to-back user agent).

The list can be contained in the request, or it can be an external list tied to the Request-URI and set up out of band, for example with XCAP. RFC 4662 describes a service for SUBSCRIBE that uses stored lists. This RFC covers both kinds.
sections.eli5: Sending one message to many people from a slow connection takes forever. A helper in the network can do the copying for you instead.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.content:
For services that take a list inside the request, REQ 1 says the invocation mechanism MUST let the invoker provide a list of destination URIs, and REQ 2 says it SHOULD NOT need more than one transaction.

Four general requirements apply to all URI-list services:

  • GEN 1: a service MAY do more than send requests. For example, an INVITE service may act as a conference server and mix media.
  • GEN 2: the meaning of the list MUST be left to the application that receives it.
  • GEN 3: the invoker MUST be able to find out the result of the operations done with the list.
  • GEN 4: a service MUST NOT send requests to any destination without authenticating the invoker.
sections.eli5: The rules say: the helper must take a whole list at once, must tell you how it went, and must check who you are before sending anything.

sections.title: Carrying URI Lists in SIP
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new disposition type for the Content-Disposition header field: recipient-list. Requests and responses MAY carry bodies of this type, and such a body lists the final recipients of the requests the service will generate.

The default list format is service specific, so each URI-list service specification MUST define a default format. Clients SHOULD NOT include the same URI more than once.

A server that receives several recipient-list body parts MUST act as if it had received one list containing all the URIs. If a URI appears more than once, the server MUST treat it as appearing once, using the comparison rules of the URI scheme. RFC 5364 covers duplicate entries tagged with different copyControl values.
sections.eli5: The list rides along in the message with a special label saying, these are the people to send this to. If a name shows up twice, the helper only sends it once.

sections.title: Processing Lists and Reporting Results
sections.content:
Because a URI-list service can be a general application server, how it interprets the list depends on the service. For a conference server the URIs might be the initial participants, and for a service handling MESSAGE they might be the recipients of an instant message. So the behavior SHOULD be specified per service. The RFC points to RFC 5366 for INVITE, RFC 5365 for MESSAGE and RFC 5367 for SUBSCRIBE.

Reporting results is also service specific. For instance, a user agent that set up an ad hoc conference with an INVITE carrying a list can learn which participants joined by using the conference package of RFC 4575.
sections.eli5: What the helper does with the list depends on the job. For a group chat it sends a message to each name, and for a conference call it rings each name.

sections.title: Security: Integrity and Authentication
sections.content:
The RFC calls security the most important common area across all URI-list services. A service takes one request in and sends out many, so attackers may try to use it as a traffic amplifier for denial-of-service attacks.

Attackers may also modify the list on its way to the server, causing requests to go to other recipients than the client intended. To prevent this, clients SHOULD integrity protect URI lists end to end with something like S/MIME or, if that is unavailable, hop by hop with TLS. Both can also give confidentiality.

Services MUST authenticate users and check authorization before any fan-out, and MUST NOT explode a request for an unauthorized user. The same applies to stored lists. A service MAY limit the number of URIs it accepts in a list. Specifications for individual methods MUST describe their own method-specific security issues.
sections.eli5: The helper must check you are really you before sending a single copy, and the list should be sealed so nobody can change the names on the way.

sections.title: Amplification Attacks and Opt-In Lists
sections.content:
An attacker may put URIs in a list whose hosts route to a victim. The victims need not be SIP nodes and can even be routers. The attacker then floods them without generating much traffic. The RFC notes that this problem also appears elsewhere, such as in multihoming scenarios.

Authentication alone does not stop authorized users from doing this, so the RFC introduces opt-in lists. A service MUST NOT send a request to a destination that has not agreed beforehand to receive requests from that service. Users can agree by filling in a web page, sending an email, signing a contract, or using the consent framework of RFC 5360. Users MUST also be able to narrow what they accept, for example only requests from a given service on behalf of a given user.

The service checks every destination in a received list. If it has permission for all of them it sends the requests, and if not, it sends no requests at all. The method for getting permissions must not itself amplify, which is why services cannot simply contact all targets to ask. To be interoperable, services MUST implement and SHOULD use RFC 5360.
sections.eli5: You can only be on the list if you said yes first. If even one name on the list has not said yes, the helper sends nothing, so nobody gets flooded with mail they did not want.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC adds one value, recipient-list, to the IANA registry for Mail Content Disposition Values and Parameters. Its description is that the body includes a list of URIs to which URI-list services are to be applied.

No other registrations are made, and the format of the list itself is left to each service specification.
sections.eli5: The new label for the list was added to the official list of labels, so everyone uses the same word.
